```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# error = TRUE lets the report knit even while some of your code is unfinished.
# Each chunk with an error shows the message in the report; fix it and Knit again.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, error = TRUE)

pkgs <- c("haven", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "broom", "lme4", "lmerTest", "knitr", "splines")
missing <- setdiff(pkgs, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(missing)) install.packages(missing, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(haven); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2)
  library(broom); library(lme4); library(lmerTest)
})

# Helpers that print model results in a consistent table
show_lm <- function(model, pattern) {
  tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(grepl(pattern, term)) |>
    select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |> knitr::kable()
}
show_glm <- function(model, pattern) {   # odds ratios (or rate ratios for Poisson)
  tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |> filter(grepl(pattern, term)) |>
    select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |> knitr::kable()
}
show_lmer <- function(model, pattern) {
  co <- summary(model)$coefficients
  co <- co[grepl(pattern, rownames(co)), , drop = FALSE]
  data.frame(term = rownames(co), estimate = co[, "Estimate"],
             conf.low = co[, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * co[, "Std. Error"],
             conf.high = co[, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * co[, "Std. Error"],
             p.value = co[, ncol(co)], row.names = NULL) |>
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |> knitr::kable()
}
```

# How to use this file {-}

1. Download `HAALSI_W1-3_Longitudinal_Dataset.dta` from the HAALSI Harvard Dataverse and put it
   in the same folder as this file. The name must match exactly (rename it if your browser
   added something like `(1)` or `_2`).
2. Click **Knit**. The first run builds a cleaned dataset (`..._long.rds`); later runs reuse it.
3. **Data cleaning** and **About the data** are done for you. Read them, but don't change them.
4. In each question, look for `___` (three underscores). Replace each one with code, then Knit again.
   Lines starting with `# HINT` tell you what goes there.
   Until you fill a blank, that chunk shows `Error: unexpected input` in the report. That's expected.
   Later chunks that use your result will also show errors until the earlier blank is done.
5. Write your answers in the *Interpretation* lines under each question.
6. Do not submit or share the `.dta` or `.rds` files.

# Data cleaning

This section reads the HAALSI file you downloaded from Harvard Dataverse, keeps the variables we need, recodes them and saves a
cleaned file with one row per person per wave. It only runs if the cleaned file doesn't exist
yet, or if you render with `params = list(rebuild = TRUE)`.

**Coding rules used below:** −97 (refused), −98 (don't know) and −99 (empty) are missing;
yes/no variables are 1 = Yes, 2 = No and are recoded to 1/0; sex is 1 = Male, 2 = Female.

```{r cleaning, error = FALSE}
dta_path <- params$data_path
rds_path <- paste0(tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(dta_path)), "_long.rds")

if (params$rebuild || !file.exists(rds_path)) {
  if (!file.exists(dta_path)) {
    stop("Cannot find '", dta_path, "'. Download it from the HAALSI Harvard Dataverse, ",
         "put it in the same folder as this .Rmd file and check the file name matches exactly.")
  }

  # 1. Variables. "?" is replaced by the wave number.
  wave_vars <- c(
    age = "w?c_rage_calc", marital_status = "w?c_bd_mar", hhsize = "w?c_hhsize",
    hhnum = "w?c_hhnum", wealth = "w?c_wealthindex", asset = "w?c_hh_assetindex",
    employment = "w?c_ep_employed",
    memory = "w?cn001", concentration = "w?cn002", learning = "w?cn003",
    cesd = "w?c_cd_cesd", bmi = "w?c_bs_bmi", bmi_category = "w?c_bs_bmicat",
    hypertension_diag = "w?c_cm_hypertension_srdiag", htn_on_med_raw = "w?cm005",
    diabetes_diag = "w?c_cm_diabetes_srdiag", dm_on_med_raw = "w?cm010",
    adls_walk = "w?c_pf_diff_walk", adls_dress = "w?c_pf_diff_dress",
    adls_bath = "w?c_pf_diff_bath", adls_eat = "w?c_pf_diff_eat",
    adls_toilet = "w?c_pf_diff_toilet",
    systolic_bp = "w?c_bs_mean_sys", diastolic_bp = "w?c_bs_mean_dia", glucose = "w?c_bs_glucose",
    smoking = "w?cm059", alcohol = "w?cm068",
    status = "w?status", int_year = "w?c_int_year", int_month = "w?c_int_month",
    # cognition (Waves 2-3 have summary scores; Wave 1 is built from item-level data below)
    imrec1 = "w?c_cn_imrec1", delrec = "w?c_cn_delrec", orient_sum = "w?cn214"
  )
  fixed_vars <- c("w2c_rsex", "w1c_bd_educ4", "w1c_bd_country")
  w1_cog_items <- c("w1cn013", paste0("w1cn007s", 1:10), paste0("w1cn012s", 1:10),
                    paste0("w1cn01", 4:7))

  wanted <- c("prim_key", fixed_vars, w1_cog_items,
              unlist(lapply(1:3, function(w) sub("?", w, wave_vars, fixed = TRUE))))
  all_names <- names(read_dta(dta_path, n_max = 0))
  raw <- read_dta(dta_path, col_select = all_of(intersect(wanted, all_names)))
  raw <- zap_labels(zap_missing(raw))

  # 2. Helpers
  neg_to_na <- function(x) { x <- as.numeric(x); x[x < 0] <- NA; x }
  yes_no    <- function(x) { x <- as.numeric(x)
    case_when(x == 1 ~ 1, x %in% c(0, 2) ~ 0, TRUE ~ NA_real_) }

  # 3. Wave 1 cognition from item-level data.
  #    Word recall: one column per word, value > 0 = word recalled.
  #    Wave 1 had one immediate-recall trial, so trial 1 is used in every wave.
  w1_recall <- function(stem) {
    m <- as.matrix(raw[, paste0(stem, "s", 1:10)]); m[is.na(m)] <- 0
    n <- rowSums(m > 0)
    n[rowSums(m == -97) > 0] <- NA            # refused
    n[is.na(raw$w1cn013)] <- NA               # cognition section not done (e.g., proxy)
    n
  }
  orient_w1 <- sapply(paste0("w1cn01", 4:7), function(v) {
    x <- as.numeric(raw[[v]]); case_when(x == 1 ~ 1, x %in% c(2, -98) ~ 0, TRUE ~ NA_real_) })
  w1_cog <- tibble(prim_key = raw$prim_key, wave = 1,
                   imrec1_w1 = w1_recall("w1cn007"), delrec_w1 = w1_recall("w1cn012"),
                   orient_w1 = rowSums(orient_w1))

  # 4. Wide -> long
  long <- lapply(1:3, function(w) {
    cols <- sub("?", w, wave_vars, fixed = TRUE)
    out  <- tibble(prim_key = raw$prim_key, wave = w)
    for (nm in names(wave_vars)) {
      out[[nm]] <- if (cols[[nm]] %in% names(raw)) as.numeric(raw[[cols[[nm]]]]) else NA_real_
    }
    out
  }) |> bind_rows() |>
    left_join(w1_cog, by = c("prim_key", "wave")) |>
    mutate(imrec1     = if_else(wave == 1, imrec1_w1, imrec1),
           delrec     = if_else(wave == 1, delrec_w1, delrec),
           orient_sum = if_else(wave == 1, orient_w1, orient_sum)) |>
    select(-imrec1_w1, -delrec_w1, -orient_w1)

  fixed <- tibble(
    prim_key = raw$prim_key,
    sex = case_when(raw$w2c_rsex == 1 ~ 1, raw$w2c_rsex == 2 ~ 0),     # 1 = Male, 0 = Female
    education_category = neg_to_na(raw$w1c_bd_educ4),
    born_moz = case_when(raw$w1c_bd_country == 2 ~ 1, raw$w1c_bd_country == 1 ~ 0)
  )

  # 5. Recode
  long <- long |>
    left_join(fixed, by = "prim_key") |>
    mutate(
      status = if_else(wave == 1, 1, status),
      across(c(age, marital_status, hhsize, hhnum, wealth, employment, memory, concentration,
               learning, cesd, bmi, bmi_category, systolic_bp, diastolic_bp, glucose,
               imrec1, delrec, orient_sum), neg_to_na),
      employment = if_else(wave == 3 & employment == 0, 2, employment),
      across(c(hypertension_diag, diabetes_diag, smoking, alcohol, htn_on_med_raw,
               dm_on_med_raw), yes_no),
      across(starts_with("adls_"), ~ case_when(.x %in% c(1, 3) ~ 1, .x == 2 ~ 0, TRUE ~ NA_real_))
    )

  # 6. Derived variables
  long <- long |>
    mutate(
      htn_group = factor(case_when(hypertension_diag == 0 ~ "No hypertension",
                                   htn_on_med_raw == 1    ~ "Hypertension, treated",
                                   hypertension_diag == 1 ~ "Hypertension, untreated"),
                         levels = c("No hypertension", "Hypertension, untreated",
                                    "Hypertension, treated")),
      dm_group  = factor(case_when(diabetes_diag == 0 ~ "No diabetes",
                                   dm_on_med_raw == 1 ~ "Diabetes, treated",
                                   diabetes_diag == 1 ~ "Diabetes, untreated"),
                         levels = c("No diabetes", "Diabetes, untreated", "Diabetes, treated")),
      adl_count = adls_walk + adls_dress + adls_bath + adls_eat + adls_toilet,
      any_adl   = as.numeric(adl_count > 0),
      int_date  = int_year + (int_month - 0.5) / 12
    ) |>
    select(-htn_on_med_raw, -dm_on_med_raw)

  # Objective cognition: each test z-scored to Wave 1, averaged, re-standardized to Wave 1.
  ref <- filter(long, wave == 1)
  zref <- function(x, r) (x - mean(r, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(r, na.rm = TRUE)
  long <- long |>
    mutate(cog_raw = (zref(orient_sum, ref$orient_sum) + zref(imrec1, ref$imrec1) +
                        zref(delrec, ref$delrec)) / 3)
  long <- long |>
    mutate(objective_cognition_z = zref(cog_raw, cog_raw[wave == 1])) |> select(-cog_raw)
  cut20 <- quantile(long$objective_cognition_z[long$wave == 1], 0.20, na.rm = TRUE)
  long  <- long |> mutate(low_cognition = as.numeric(objective_cognition_z < cut20))

  # Wealth: asset index in SD units (Wave 1 scale); CES-D z-scored within wave
  long <- long |>
    mutate(asset_sd = zref(asset, asset[wave == 1])) |>
    group_by(wave) |>
    mutate(cesd_z = (cesd - mean(cesd, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(cesd, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    ungroup()

  # Time since baseline (Wave 1) interview, in years
  long <- long |>
    group_by(prim_key) |>
    mutate(years_since_bl = int_date - int_date[wave == 1][1]) |>
    ungroup()

  # Labelled factors
  long <- long |>
    mutate(
      sex_f       = factor(sex, 0:1, c("Female", "Male")),
      education_f = factor(education_category, 1:4,
                           c("No formal", "Some primary", "Some secondary", "Secondary+")),
      marital_f   = factor(marital_status, 0:3,
                           c("Never married", "Separated/divorced", "Widowed", "Married")),
      hhsize_f    = factor(hhsize, 0:3, c("Alone", "2 people", "3-6 people", "7+ people")),
      wealth_f    = factor(wealth, 1:5, c("Q1 (poorest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q5 (richest)")),
      employment_f   = factor(employment, 1:3, c("Employed", "Not working", "Homemaker")),
      bmi_category_f = factor(bmi_category, 0:3, c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
    ) |>
    arrange(prim_key, wave)

  saveRDS(long, rds_path)
}

haalsi <- readRDS(rds_path)
cat(rds_path, ":", nrow(haalsi), "person-waves,", n_distinct(haalsi$prim_key), "participants\n")
```

# About the data

* `objective_cognition_z` is available in **all three waves**. It averages orientation (0–4),
  immediate word recall (trial 1, 0–10) and delayed word recall (0–10), each scaled to Wave 1.
  0 = the Wave 1 average; 1 = one Wave 1 standard deviation. `low_cognition` = below the Wave 1
  20th percentile.
* Cross-sectional questions use **Wave 1** (`w1`), the largest sample with full covariates.
  Change over time uses all three waves (`cog_long`), with `years_since_bl` = years since the
  Wave 1 interview (about 3 years to Wave 2, about 6 to Wave 3).
* Wealth: `wealth_f` = asset-index quintile; `asset_sd` = the continuous asset index in SD units.
* CES-D is the 8-item scale in Wave 1 (0–8) and the 20-item scale in Waves 2–3. `cesd_z` is
  standardized within wave. We use the Wave 1 score.
* `htn_group` and `dm_group` compare no condition / untreated / treated. Treatment comes from the
  "on treatment" questions, *not* from `_srtrt` (which is a narrower definition of the condition).
* Self-reported cognition is coded so higher = worse (memory: 1 = excellent … 5 = poor;
  concentration and learning: 1 = no difficulty … 5 = extreme).
* Average scores rise slightly over follow-up because people get better at repeated tests, and
  about 1 in 5 participants died by Wave 3. Interpret **differences in change between groups**,
  not the average change.

```{r about, error = FALSE}
haalsi |>
  group_by(wave) |>
  summarise(completed = sum(status == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            with_cognition = sum(!is.na(objective_cognition_z)),
            mean_years_since_bl = round(mean(years_since_bl[status == 1], na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            mean_cognition = round(mean(objective_cognition_z, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()

w1 <- filter(haalsi, wave == 1) |> mutate(bmi_category_f = relevel(bmi_category_f, ref = "Normal"))

# Baseline (Wave 1) characteristics, used as predictors of change
baseline <- w1 |>
  transmute(prim_key, age_bl = age, age10_bl = (age - 60) / 10, sex_f, education_f, born_moz,
            marital_f, hhsize_bl_f = hhsize_f, wealth_bl = wealth, asset_sd_bl = asset_sd,
            employment_bl_f = employment_f, cesd_bl_z = cesd_z,
            htn_bl = hypertension_diag, htn_group_bl = htn_group, dm_bl = diabetes_diag,
            bmi_bl = bmi, bmi_cat_bl_f = bmi_category_f, smoking_bl = smoking, alcohol_bl = alcohol)

# One row per person per wave with cognition, plus baseline characteristics
cog_long <- haalsi |>
  filter(!is.na(objective_cognition_z), !is.na(years_since_bl)) |>
  select(prim_key, wave, years = years_since_bl, objective_cognition_z, low_cognition) |>
  left_join(baseline, by = "prim_key")

cat("Wave 1 sample:", nrow(w1), " | person-waves with cognition:", nrow(cog_long), "\n")
```

# Question 1: Which intervention could have the greatest benefit?

## 1a. Is household wealth associated with cognition? (worked example)

This section is complete. Use it as a model for the rest of the questions.

**Confounders.** Age and sex influence wealth and cognition, and education comes before
wealth in the life course. Avoid variables that wealth itself could change (BMI, hypertension,
depression), since they may be mechanisms.

```{r q1a}
# Level of cognition: wealth quintiles vs the poorest, and per SD of the asset index
m1a_cat <- lm(objective_cognition_z ~ wealth_f + age + sex_f + education_f, data = w1)
show_lm(m1a_cat, "wealth")

m1a_sd <- lm(objective_cognition_z ~ asset_sd + age + sex_f + education_f, data = w1)
show_lm(m1a_sd, "asset")

# Risk of low cognition: odds ratios
m1a_low <- glm(low_cognition ~ asset_sd + age + sex_f + education_f, family = binomial, data = w1)
show_glm(m1a_low, "asset")

# Rate of change: random intercept and slope per person.
# Covariates interact with time so they adjust the slope as well as the level.
m1a_slope <- lmer(objective_cognition_z ~ years * (asset_sd_bl + age10_bl + sex_f + education_f) +
                    (1 + years | prim_key), data = cog_long)
show_lmer(m1a_slope, "asset")
```

*Interpretation:* Cognition rises steadily with wealth. Compared with the poorest quintile, Q2 scores
0.09 SD higher and the richest quintile 0.31 SD higher (95% CI 0.23 to 0.39), after age, sex and
education. Each 1 SD of the asset index is worth 0.11 SD of cognition and lowers the odds of low
cognition by about 30% (OR 0.70, 0.63 to 0.78). Wealth does not predict the rate of change
(`years:asset_sd_bl` = 0.002 SD/year, CI -0.004 to 0.007): it is tied to the level of cognition,
not how fast it changes over 6 years.

*Try:* add `log(hhnum)` (household size) or `marital_f`. Is each a confounder or a mediator?

## 1b. Is hypertension associated with cognition?

Compare no hypertension, untreated hypertension and treated hypertension (`htn_group`).

```{r q1b}
# Level of cognition
# HINT: put the exposure where the ___ is. Which confounders? Is wealth a confounder here?
m1b <- lm(objective_cognition_z ~ htn_group + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f, data = w1)
show_lm(m1b, "htn")

```

```{r q1b-low}
# Risk of low cognition
# HINT: outcome = low_cognition; logistic regression uses family = binomial
m1b_low <- glm(low_cognition ~ htn_group + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f, family = binomial, data = w1)
show_glm(m1b_low, "htn")

```

```{r q1b-slope}
# Rate of change
# HINT: copy m1a_slope above and replace asset_sd_bl with htn_group_bl
m1b_slope <- lmer(objective_cognition_z ~ years * (htn_group_bl + age10_bl + sex_f + education_f + asset_sd_bl) +
                    (1 + years | prim_key), data = cog_long)
show_lmer(m1b_slope, "htn")
```

*Interpretation:* Untreated hypertension looks just like no hypertension (+0.01 SD, CI -0.04 to
0.07; OR 1.01). Treated hypertension scores 0.16 SD *higher* (CI 0.10 to 0.22), with lower odds of
low cognition (OR 0.61, 0.50 to 0.76). That is very unlikely to be the pills alone. People who get
diagnosed and treated are the ones who reach clinics, follow up and have the means and health
literacy to do so (healthy-user and access-to-care confounding). Wealth and education only partly
capture that. The treated group's slope is slightly steeper (-0.020 SD/year, CI -0.033 to -0.007),
consistent with regression to the mean from a higher starting point, not harm. This is not causal
evidence that treatment protects cognition. The fair comparison would be a trial or a
treatment-access natural experiment.

## 1c. Is depression associated with objective and subjective cognition?

All outcomes are standardized so the coefficients can be compared. For subjective outcomes a
positive coefficient means more reported difficulty; for objective cognition a negative
coefficient means worse performance.

```{r q1c}
w1_std <- w1 |>
  mutate(across(c(objective_cognition_z, memory, concentration, learning),
                ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)), .names = "{.col}_std"))
outcomes <- c("objective_cognition_z_std", "memory_std", "concentration_std", "learning_std")

```

```{r q1c-loop}
q1c <- lapply(outcomes, function(y) {
  # HINT: the exposure is the standardized CES-D score. Use the same name in both blanks.
  f <- reformulate(c("cesd_z", "age", "sex_f", "education_f", "wealth_f"), response = y)
  tidy(lm(f, data = w1_std), conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "cesd_z") |> mutate(outcome = y)
}) |> bind_rows()

q1c |> select(outcome, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |> knitr::kable()

```

```{r q1c-low}
# YOUR TURN: fit a logistic model of low_cognition on cesd_z (same covariates) and show the OR.
m1c_low <- glm(low_cognition ~ cesd_z + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f, family = binomial, data = w1)
show_glm(m1c_low, "cesd")
```

*Interpretation:* A 1 SD higher CES-D score goes with 0.11 SD *lower* objective cognition but
0.17 to 0.20 SD *more* self-reported difficulty (memory 0.20, concentration 0.18, learning 0.17),
so the subjective link is almost twice the objective one. Each SD of CES-D also raises the odds of
low cognition by 26% (OR 1.26, 1.17 to 1.36). Depressed people report more cognitive trouble than
their test scores show, so self-reports used for screening would over-flag people with depressive
symptoms. Depression and cognition can also cause each other (reverse causation).

## 1d. Putting it together: how much could each intervention reduce low cognition?

`prev_shift()` sets everyone's exposure to a post-intervention value, predicts each person's
probability of low cognition and compares the average with the baseline. The cash-transfer
scenario is done. Write the other two and justify every assumption.

```{r q1d}
prev_shift <- function(model, change) {
  d0 <- model.frame(model) |> as.data.frame()
  d1 <- change(d0)
  c(before = mean(predict(model, d0, type = "response")),
    after  = mean(predict(model, d1, type = "response")))
}

scenarios <- list(
  # Cash transfer: assets up by 0.5 SD (justify using the Old Age Pension literature)
  "Cash transfer: assets +0.5 SD" =
    prev_shift(m1a_low, function(d) mutate(d, asset_sd = asset_sd + 0.5))
)
```

```{r q1d-yours}
scenarios <- c(scenarios, list(
  # HINT: use m1b_low. Change everyone in "Hypertension, untreated" to "Hypertension, treated".
  "HTN care: treat all untreated hypertension" =
    prev_shift(m1b_low, function(d) mutate(d, htn_group = replace(htn_group, htn_group == "Hypertension, untreated", "Hypertension, treated"))),

  # HINT: use m1c_low. Lower cesd_z by 0.5, but only for people with cesd_z > 0 (symptomatic).
  "Psychotherapy: CES-D -0.5 SD if symptomatic" =
    prev_shift(m1c_low, function(d) mutate(d, cesd_z = ifelse(cesd_z > 0, cesd_z - 0.5, cesd_z)))
))
```

```{r q1d-table}

do.call(rbind, scenarios) |> as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(change_pct_points = round(100 * (after - before), 2),
         before = round(100 * before, 1), after = round(100 * after, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Low cognition before (%)", "After (%)", "Change (percentage points)"))
```

*Discussion:*

* **Results:** with about 20% of people in low cognition at baseline, a 0.5 SD rise in assets
  lowers predicted prevalence by 2.2 percentage points (19.9% to 17.8%). Treating all untreated
  hypertension lowers it by 2.1 points. Reducing CES-D by 0.5 SD in symptomatic people lowers it
  by 0.6 points. The depression row starts at 19.8% instead of 19.9% because people missing
  CES-D drop out of that model.
* **Is +0.5 SD plausible?** South Africa's Old Age Pension is large relative to household income
  in rural areas. Case (2001) and Duflo (2003) show it changed health and nutrition across the
  household, and Ardington et al. (2009) show it changed household composition and labour. So a
  sustained transfer could plausibly move durable assets by a meaningful fraction of an SD. But an
  asset index moves slowly, and 0.5 SD is optimistic for a short program.
* **What would make these causal?** No unmeasured confounding of exposure and cognition, correct
  model form, and an intervention that moves the exposure the same way the natural variation
  did. **We trust the hypertension estimate least.** Untreated hypertension shows no deficit, so
  the whole "benefit" comes from comparing treated with untreated people, who differ in access
  to care and health behaviour (see 1b). The wealth estimate is also confounded (childhood
  circumstances, lifelong cognitive ability) but has a quasi-experimental literature behind it.
* **Most promising:** a cash transfer / financial-security intervention. It has the largest
  modelled effect, the most credible mechanism and existing natural-experiment evidence. It also
  helps the whole household. Hypertension care is worth doing for heart and stroke reasons, but
  these data do not show it protects cognition. Other approaches: education is the strongest
  correlate of cognitive level here, so investing in schooling helps future cohorts. Hearing and
  vision correction and treating depression for its own sake are also candidates.

# Question 2: Is self-reported memory associated with objective cognition?

```{r q2}
w1 |>
  select(objective_cognition_z, memory, concentration, learning) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman") |>
  round(2) |> knitr::kable(caption = "Spearman correlations (Wave 1)")

```

```{r q2-model}
# YOUR TURN 1: regress objective_cognition_z on factor(memory) plus age, sex_f, education_f
m2 <- lm(objective_cognition_z ~ factor(memory) + age + sex_f + education_f, data = w1)
show_lm(m2, "memory")

```

```{r q2-screen}
# YOUR TURN 2: how well does rating memory "fair" or "poor" (memory >= 4) identify people with
# low_cognition? Make a 2x2 table and calculate sensitivity and specificity.
# HINT: table(w1$memory >= 4, w1$low_cognition)
tab2 <- table(fair_or_poor = w1$memory >= 4, low_cognition = w1$low_cognition)
tab2
c(sensitivity = tab2["TRUE", "1"] / sum(tab2[, "1"]),
  specificity = tab2["FALSE", "0"] / sum(tab2[, "0"]),
  ppv = tab2["TRUE", "1"] / sum(tab2["TRUE", ])) |> round(3)
```

*Interpretation:* Self-rated memory is clearly related to test scores. Each step worse goes with
lower cognition, and "poor" memory scores 1.18 SD below "excellent". But the Spearman correlation is
only -0.38. As a screen, rating memory fair or poor catches just **37%** of people with low
cognition (sensitivity 0.37), so it misses nearly two in three. Only 40% of those it flags are
actually low (PPV 0.40, against a 20% base rate). Specificity is 0.86. It is a weak substitute for
a short objective test, though it is better than nothing where testing is impossible.

# Question 3: Is diabetes associated with objective and subjective cognition?

```{r q3}
# YOUR TURN: repeat the Q1c loop with dm_group as the exposure.
# HINT: copy the q1c code, replace "cesd_z" with "dm_group", and filter with grepl("dm_group", term)
q3 <- lapply(outcomes, function(y) {
  f <- reformulate(c("dm_group", "age", "sex_f", "education_f", "wealth_f"), response = y)
  tidy(lm(f, data = w1_std), conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(grepl("dm_group", term)) |> mutate(outcome = y)
}) |> bind_rows()

q3 |> select(outcome, term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |> knitr::kable()
w1 |> count(dm_group) |> knitr::kable()
```

*Interpretation:* Yes. Objective cognition is not different with diabetes (untreated -0.07 SD,
CI -0.17 to 0.03; treated -0.02, CI -0.13 to 0.09). But people with diabetes rate their memory
worse (+0.13 SD in both groups, both CIs above 0) and report more learning difficulty (untreated
+0.12). Diabetes affects how people perceive their cognition more than measured performance, which
could reflect fatigue, low mood or symptoms of high or low blood sugar. Only 249 treated and 310
untreated people (407 missing), so confidence intervals are wide and the treated-vs-untreated
contrast can't be interpreted. We can't rule out a small objective effect.

# Question 4: Is BMI category associated with objective cognition?

`bmi_category_f` has Normal as the reference group.

```{r q4}
# YOUR TURN 1: regress objective_cognition_z on bmi_category_f with your chosen confounders
m4 <- lm(objective_cognition_z ~ bmi_category_f + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f, data = w1)
show_lm(m4, "bmi")

```

```{r q4-plot}
w1_cc <- w1 |> drop_na(objective_cognition_z, bmi, age, sex_f, education_f, wealth_f)
ggplot(filter(w1_cc, bmi > 12, bmi < 55), aes(bmi, objective_cognition_z)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess") + labs(x = "BMI", y = "Objective cognition (z)")
```

```{r q4-spline}
# YOUR TURN 2: is the association with continuous BMI non-linear?
# HINT: compare lm(... ~ bmi + ...) with lm(... ~ splines::ns(bmi, 3) + ...) using anova().
# Both models must use the same rows, so use data = w1_cc.
m4_lin <- lm(objective_cognition_z ~ bmi + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f, data = w1_cc)
m4_ns  <- lm(objective_cognition_z ~ splines::ns(bmi, 3) + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f, data = w1_cc)
anova(m4_lin, m4_ns)

# Moderation by hypertension (HIV status is not in this file)
m4_int <- lm(objective_cognition_z ~ bmi_category_f * hypertension_diag + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f,
             data = w1)
anova(lm(objective_cognition_z ~ bmi_category_f + hypertension_diag + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f,
         data = model.frame(m4_int)), m4_int)
```

*Interpretation:* Relative to normal BMI, underweight people score 0.20 SD lower (CI -0.31 to
-0.09), overweight 0.13 SD higher and obese 0.20 SD higher. Within the observed range the
association rises with BMI, but a spline fits better than a straight line (F = 11.4, p < 0.001):
the curve is steep at low BMI and flattens higher up. Being thin at older ages is often a
*consequence* of illness, food insecurity or early dementia (reverse causation), and being heavy
can mark household resources. So this should not be read as "weight gain protects the brain".
Moderation by hypertension is null (interaction F = 0.88, p = 0.45).

# Question 5: Are hypertension and diabetes associated with functional disability?

```{r q5}
w1_adl <- w1 |>
  mutate(comorbidity = factor(case_when(
    hypertension_diag == 0 & diabetes_diag == 0 ~ "Neither",
    hypertension_diag == 1 & diabetes_diag == 0 ~ "Hypertension only",
    hypertension_diag == 0 & diabetes_diag == 1 ~ "Diabetes only",
    hypertension_diag == 1 & diabetes_diag == 1 ~ "Both"),
    levels = c("Neither", "Hypertension only", "Diabetes only", "Both")))
w1_adl |> count(comorbidity) |> knitr::kable()

adl_outcomes <- c("adls_walk", "adls_dress", "adls_bath", "adls_eat", "adls_toilet", "any_adl")
sapply(w1_adl[adl_outcomes], mean, na.rm = TRUE) |> round(3)   # prevalence: some are rare

```

```{r q5-models}
# YOUR TURN 1: for each ADL outcome, fit a logistic model with comorbidity + confounders
# and keep the comorbidity odds ratios.
# HINT: same structure as the Q1c loop; use glm(f, family = binomial, data = w1_adl)
# and tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE)
q5 <- lapply(adl_outcomes, function(y) {
  f <- reformulate(c("comorbidity", "age", "sex_f", "education_f", "wealth_f"), response = y)
  tidy(glm(f, family = binomial, data = w1_adl), conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
    filter(grepl("comorbidity", term)) |> mutate(outcome = y)
}) |> bind_rows()

q5 |> select(outcome, term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |> knitr::kable()

```

```{r q5-interaction}
# YOUR TURN 2: is having both conditions worse than expected from each alone?
# HINT: glm(any_adl ~ hypertension_diag * diabetes_diag + ..., family = binomial) and look at
# the interaction term.
m5_int <- glm(any_adl ~ hypertension_diag * diabetes_diag + age + sex_f + education_f + wealth_f,
              family = binomial, data = w1_adl)
show_glm(m5_int, "hypertension|diabetes")
```

*Interpretation:* Hypertension alone shows no excess ADL difficulty (any ADL OR 1.00, 0.78 to 1.29).
Diabetes alone is imprecise (only 117 people). Having **both** about doubles the odds of any ADL
difficulty (OR 2.02, 1.42 to 2.85), with similar results for walking (2.07) and toileting (2.19)
and a weaker one for dressing (1.83). Bathing and eating are not clearly raised. The eating row for
"Diabetes only" is unusable (OR 0, CI to 18,000: no events in that cell). The interaction term (OR
1.49, 0.75 to 3.15) is underpowered: the data fit a combined effect at least as large as the
two conditions added together, but can't tell whether it is more than that. Comorbidity may also
stand in for longer disease duration or complications.

# Question 6: Which baseline factors predict cognitive decline?

Each factor's interaction with `years` shows whether it predicts faster (negative) or slower
(positive) change, in SD per year.

```{r q6}
# YOUR TURN: add the other baseline predictors inside the parentheses.
# Available: age10_bl, sex_f, education_f, asset_sd_bl, cesd_bl_z, htn_bl, dm_bl,
#            bmi_cat_bl_f, smoking_bl, alcohol_bl
m6 <- lmer(objective_cognition_z ~ years * (age10_bl + sex_f + education_f + asset_sd_bl + cesd_bl_z + htn_bl + dm_bl +
                                         bmi_cat_bl_f + smoking_bl + alcohol_bl) + (1 + years | prim_key),
           data = cog_long)
show_lmer(m6, "^years")
```

*Interpretation:*

* Average scores *rise* by 0.08 SD/year (people improve with retesting), so read every
  interaction as a smaller or larger gain, not true decline. Older age predicts a smaller gain
  (-0.013 SD/year per decade). More education predicts a smaller gain (secondary+ -0.08 SD/year).
  Higher baseline depressive symptoms predict a slightly *larger* gain (+0.009). Wealth,
  hypertension, diabetes, BMI, smoking and alcohol do not predict the slope.
* The education result is a ceiling, practice-effect and regression-to-the-mean artefact. More
  educated people start near the top of a short test and have less room to improve. The CES-D
  result is the mirror image: people tested on a bad day bounce back. Neither should be read as
  education being harmful or depression being protective.
* Dropout and death (about 1 in 5 by Wave 3) remove people who were declining fastest. The
  survivors look better than the cohort, which hides real decline in high-risk groups.
* The random-slope variance is close to zero ("singular fit"), so most variation is in levels,
  not slopes. Fixed effects are what we interpret.

# Question 7: Who is most resilient to cognitive decline?

**Approach A:** interactions with time, focused on possible protective factors.

```{r q7a}
# YOUR TURN: same as m6, using education_f, asset_sd_bl, employment_bl_f, cesd_bl_z, htn_bl,
# dm_bl, bmi_bl inside the parentheses, and age10_bl + sex_f outside.
m7 <- lmer(objective_cognition_z ~ age10_bl + sex_f +
             years * (education_f + asset_sd_bl + employment_bl_f + cesd_bl_z + htn_bl + dm_bl + bmi_bl) +
             (1 + years | prim_key), data = cog_long)
show_lmer(m7, "^years")
```

**Approach B:** among people with cognition at Waves 1 and 3, predict Wave 3 cognition from
Wave 1 cognition, age, sex and follow-up time. People in the top 20% of residuals (doing better
than expected) are labelled resilient.

```{r q7b}
resil <- cog_long |>
  filter(wave %in% c(1, 3)) |>
  select(prim_key, wave, objective_cognition_z, years) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = wave, values_from = c(objective_cognition_z, years)) |>
  rename(cog_w1 = objective_cognition_z_1, cog_w3 = objective_cognition_z_3, years_w3 = years_3) |>
  filter(!is.na(cog_w1), !is.na(cog_w3)) |>
  left_join(baseline, by = "prim_key")

m_resid <- lm(cog_w3 ~ cog_w1 + age_bl + I(age_bl^2) + sex_f + years_w3, data = resil)
resil$resid <- NA
resil$resid[as.numeric(rownames(model.frame(m_resid)))] <- resid(m_resid)
resil <- resil |> mutate(resilient = as.numeric(resid >= quantile(resid, 0.8, na.rm = TRUE)))

```

```{r q7b-compare}
# YOUR TURN 1: compare baseline characteristics of resilient people with everyone else
# HINT: group_by(resilient) |> summarise(n = n(), mean(asset_sd_bl, na.rm = TRUE), ...)
resil |> filter(!is.na(resilient)) |> group_by(resilient) |>
  summarise(n = n(), age = mean(age_bl, na.rm = TRUE), cog_w1 = mean(cog_w1, na.rm = TRUE),
            assets_sd = mean(asset_sd_bl, na.rm = TRUE), cesd_z = mean(cesd_bl_z, na.rm = TRUE),
            hypertension = mean(htn_bl, na.rm = TRUE), diabetes = mean(dm_bl, na.rm = TRUE),
            bmi = mean(bmi_bl, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) |> knitr::kable()

resil |> filter(!is.na(resilient)) |> with(table(education_f, resilient)) |>
  prop.table(2) |> round(2) |> knitr::kable(caption = "Education by resilience (column %)")

```

```{r q7b-model}
# YOUR TURN 2: logistic regression of resilient on the possible protective factors
m7b <- glm(resilient ~ education_f + asset_sd_bl + employment_bl_f + cesd_bl_z + htn_bl + dm_bl + bmi_bl,
           family = binomial, data = resil)
show_glm(m7b, "^(education|asset|employment|cesd|htn|dm|bmi)")
```

*Interpretation:* In Approach B, wealth is the clearest marker of resilience. Each SD of assets
raises the odds of doing better than expected by 25% (OR 1.25, 1.14 to 1.38), and some secondary
education helps too (OR 1.43, 1.07 to 1.89), though not monotonically (secondary+ OR 0.75,
CI 0.50 to 1.10). Depression, hypertension, diabetes, BMI and employment
do not distinguish the groups. **The two approaches disagree on wealth:** in Approach A,
wealth does not change the slope (0.002, p = 0.60), and education looks harmful there for the
ceiling reasons above. Resilient people started *lower* at Wave 1 (0.00 vs 0.18 SD). Because one
test score is measured with error, the residual approach still partly picks up people whose
Wave 1 score was unluckily low (regression to the mean). Everyone here survived and stayed in to
Wave 3, so the comparison group is already healthier than the cohort. Calling this "resilience"
is generous: it is "outperforming one's predicted score among survivors".

# Conclusions

* **Most promising: financial security.** Wealth has a graded link to cognitive level (richest vs
  poorest quintile +0.31 SD), and +0.5 SD of assets cuts predicted low cognition by about 2
  percentage points (about 11% of cases). It also predicts outperforming one's expected score by
  Wave 3. Hypertension treatment shows a similar modelled effect, but it rests entirely on a
  treated-vs-untreated contrast we don't trust. Depression treatment gives about 0.6 points.
* **Biggest threats:** for wealth, lifelong confounding (childhood conditions and cognitive
  ability shape both wealth and test scores). For hypertension, healthy-user and access-to-care
  bias. For depression, reverse causation. For all change analyses, practice effects and dropout
  or death.
* **Other approaches:** education is the strongest correlate of cognitive level. Diabetes
  mainly changes *perceived* cognition, so patient-centred diabetes care matters. Comorbid
  hypertension plus diabetes doubles functional-limitation odds, which argues for joint chronic
  disease management.
* **A better study:** a regression discontinuity at pension eligibility age (60) comparing
  cognition just above and below the threshold, or a randomized cash transfer with cognitive
  follow-up.
